Universality of critical phenomena

Words: 50
Critical phenomenon OurBigBook.com
Universality of critical phenomena is the agreement of critical exponents or normalized scaling forms between microscopically different systems. Dimension, symmetry and interaction range help determine the universality class. A renormalization-group flow can explain this agreement by showing that different microscopic models approach the same fixed-point description, while irrelevant differences fade at large scales.

Thermodynamic critical point

Words: 116 Articles: 3
Critical phenomenon OurBigBook.com
At an ordinary thermodynamic critical point, two coexisting phases become indistinguishable: their order parameter difference vanishes, and the correlation length and appropriate response functions typically diverge. A continuous phase transition can be approached there by tuning the thermal and conjugate-field variables. A renormalization-group fixed point controls its singular long-distance behavior. A triple point with three separated minima is not an ordinary thermodynamic critical point, and a tricritical point requires an additional tuning and has a different scaling theory.

Critical point of a cubic density equation of state

Words: 29 Articles: 1
Thermodynamic critical point OurBigBook.com
For p=nkB​T−bn2/2+cn3/6 with b,c>0, the first two density derivatives vanish at nc​=b/c, kB​Tc​=b2/(2c) and pc​=b3/(6c2). The scaled equation is p/pc​=x3−3x2+3tx, with x=n/nc​ and t=T/Tc​.

Critical concentration (cc​)

Words: 21
Thermodynamic critical point OurBigBook.com
The composition coordinate at the critical endpoint where coexisting phases become identical. Its value depends on the system and control parameters.

Lifshitz point (K(p)∼p⊥2​+p∥4​)

Words: 97 Articles: 1
Critical phenomenon OurBigBook.com
A multicritical point where disordered, spatially uniform ordered and spatially modulated phases meet. The quadratic stiffness in one or more directions vanishes, so a positive higher-derivative term stabilises the Landau-Ginzburg theory. For a uniaxial case the kernel at the point has p⊥2​+p∥4​, with the coefficient of p∥2​ tuned to zero.

Uniaxial Lifshitz Gaussian renormalization (c=b1/2,Z=b(2D+3)/4)

Words: 47
Lifshitz point OurBigBook.com
For kernel κ−1p⊥2​+μ−1p∥4​+m2 with positive stiffnesses, preserve both derivative coefficients by q⊥​=bp⊥​ and q∥​=b1/2p∥​. The Fourier field multiplier is Z=b(2D+3)/4, the mass becomes bm, and a uniform source becomes b(2D+3)/4h. The anisotropic effective dimension is D−1/2 and the Gaussian exponents are α=9/4−D/2, Δ=(2D+3)/8.

Liquid-gas critical point ((Tc​,pc​,vc​))

Words: 38 Articles: 1
Critical phenomenon OurBigBook.com
The endpoint of a gas-liquid phase coexistence curve, where the distinct liquid and gas states merge. For a smooth fluid equation of state, the critical isotherm has pv​=pvv​=0 at this point; this thermodynamic meaning differs from a stationary critical point of an arbitrary function.

Quantum critical point

Words: 107 Articles: 3
Critical phenomenon OurBigBook.com
A quantum critical point is a continuous zero-temperature phase transition driven by a nonthermal control parameter. Quantum and thermal fluctuations near it are organized by a dynamical critical exponent.

Quantum-critical regime

Words: 32
Quantum critical point OurBigBook.com
The quantum-critical regime is the finite-temperature region in which temperature exceeds the energy scale generated by detuning from a quantum critical point. Temperature then controls leading masses, relaxation rates, and correlation lengths.

Quantum critical scaling

Words: 46 Articles: 1
Quantum critical point OurBigBook.com
Quantum critical scaling expresses observables as powers of temperature or detuning times universal functions of dimensionless ratios such as ω/T, vk/T, and Δ/T.

Dynamical critical exponent (z)

Words: 20
Quantum critical scaling OurBigBook.com
The dynamical critical exponent relates critical frequency and wavenumber scales by ω∼kz. Relativistic critical theories have z=1.

Phase transition

Words: 2k Articles: 46
Critical phenomenon OurBigBook.com
A phase transition is a nonanalytic change in equilibrium behavior as a thermodynamic control parameter varies. A continuous phase transition has a diverging correlation length and no latent heat.

Crystallization

Words: 29
Phase transition OurBigBook.com
Formation of a crystal from a disordered phase. In a cooling white dwarf, crystallization of the ionic interior releases latent heat and can redistribute chemical species, affecting the relation between luminosity and white-dwarf cooling age.

Reconstructive transformation

Words: 40
Phase transition OurBigBook.com
A structural phase change requiring substantial rearrangement of near-neighbor bonding or connectivity. Its activation barriers can make equilibrium transitions kinetically sluggish. It is distinguished from a cooperative displacive transformation, rather than defined solely by the presence of a different final symmetry.

Hexatic phase

Words: 25
Phase transition OurBigBook.com
A two-dimensional phase with quasi-long-range sixfold bond-orientational order but short-range translational order. A cell model of independent particle cages does not capture its full physics.

Displacive transformation

Words: 25
Phase transition OurBigBook.com
A cooperative change of atomic positions and lattice shape without the long-range compositional diffusion required by a diffusional transformation. Tetragonal-to-monoclinic transformation in zirconia is a nonmetallic example.

Vitrification

These critical exponents describe the leading singular powers of percolation probability, percolation susceptibility, correlation length and critical cluster distributions near the percolation critical probability. Their existence and exact values require theorems or scaling hypotheses for the particular model; they are not consequences of the definition of the threshold. For θ(p)=Pp​(0↔∞) and χ(p)=Ep​∣C(0)∣, the definitions are θ(p)=(p−pc​)β+o(1) above pc​ and χ(p)=(pc​−p)−γ+o(1) below pc​. The correlation length has ξ(p)=∣p−pc​∣−ν+o(1). At criticality, the root-cluster tail is P(∣C(0)∣≥s)=s−1/δ+o(1); two-point connectivity has leading power ∣x∣−(d−2+η); and the expected number per site of size-s clusters has leading power s−τ. The last distribution differs from the size-weighted distribution seen at a specified site. Relations such as γ=(2−η)ν and 2β+γ=dν have specific scaling regimes, and the latter hyperscaling relation fails in ordinary mean-field regimes above the upper critical dimension of percolation.

Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Lower critical dimension OurBigBook.com
The Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition in the two-dimensional XY model separates a low-temperature phase with algebraically decaying correlations from a high-temperature phase with unbound vortices and exponentially decaying correlations. It does not produce conventional long-range order.
How can something resist a twist when its orientation never settles down? The distinction is between long-range order, a nonzero limiting correlation function, and phase stiffness, a free energy cost for a slow spatial twist. In a uniform two-dimensional XY model at positive temperature, smooth spin waves can erase the first while leaving the second finite. Vortex-antivortex binding then decides whether that resistance survives on arbitrarily large scales.
Vadim Lvovich Berezinskii developed an earlier description of two-dimensional order. John Michael Kosterlitz and D. J. Thouless independently developed the defect mechanism; Kosterlitz's 2016 lecture explicitly acknowledges their initial ignorance of Berezinskii's work. The central step was to include rare vortices alongside smooth spin waves.[ref]
The Mermin-Wagner theorem concerns continuous symmetry and sufficiently short-range interactions in the thermodynamic limit. It does not say that every two-dimensional system is disordered in every sense, nor that every continuous symmetry gives a Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition. Here the order parameter has a circular phase, permitting integer winding numbers. Finite-scale vortex renormalization explains why a finite sample can look coherent even when its infinite counterpart lacks long-range order.

Ev​=Ec​+2ρs​​∫aL​r22πrdr​=Ec​+πρs​log(L/a).
(2)

For L/a=1000 and Ec​/(kB​T)=2, the dimensionless free energy cost is about 5.546 at K=0.8 and −0.965 at K=0.5. The same logarithm appears in the cost and the positional reward: increasing the system size strengthens whichever has the larger coefficient. The corresponding one-defect Boltzmann factors, about 0.00390 and 2.62, are relative statistical weights, not normalized probabilities. The latter signals failure of a dilute single-defect estimate.
A single net phase vortex requires compatible boundaries: on a periodic sample use neutral pairs, as required by vortex charge neutrality. This argument identifies a possible threshold, but predicting the universal stiffness jump requires the renormalized phase stiffness, after smaller pairs have responded. It does not justify setting the transition temperature equal to a bare lattice coupling divided by a universal constant.

The four-point correlation function measures a time-ordered product of four field insertions. For a centered scalar field its disconnected terms are the three products of two-point functions, and subtracting those products leaves the connected correlation function. The uniform mode of a pure Gaussian field theory with negative squared mass has an unbounded quadratic energy. A stabilizing quartic interaction is relevant below four dimensions and ordinarily changes the critical theory to the Wilson-Fisher fixed point; above four its coefficient is a dangerously irrelevant coupling for the ordered phase.

The minimized singular free-energy density is −∣r∣3/2/(3v​) below and zero above. Fluctuations change the result below the tricritical upper critical dimension three, and marginal corrections can add logarithms at three.

Renormalization group

Words: 5k Articles: 72
Critical phenomenon OurBigBook.com
A renormalization group compares models at different observation lengths. A Wilsonian coarse-grained statistical Hamiltonian sums over short-distance fluctuations; a renormalization-group transformation rescales coordinates and fields for comparison. Kenneth Geddes Wilson's 1982 lecture treats fluctuations across successive length scales to explain critical phenomena.[ref]
The experimental motivation is Andrews's carbon dioxide experiment. Dried carbon dioxide occupied a capillary tube above mercury; a screw compressed the transmitting water. A second air-filled tube gauged pressure. Flowing water controlled temperature, and a cathetometer read column positions for volume. The liquid meniscus vanished near the liquid-gas critical point. Residual air and imperfect air-gauge corrections limited accuracy.[ref] These observations motivate critical-point theory without determining a correlation-length critical exponent. The renormalization group explains how critical measurements can become insensitive to many molecular details.
In 1972, Kenneth Geddes Wilson and Michael Ellis Fisher used an epsilon expansion about d=4 to compute nonclassical critical exponents. Their paper distinguishes a Gaussian fixed point from an interacting renormalization-group fixed point, tunes the thermal parameter, and extracts powers from a linearized recursion. Its Ising-like result is γ=1+ϵ/6+O(ϵ2) for d=4−ϵ.[ref] The worked model below isolates this mechanism with chosen coefficients; it is not a precision calculation for the three-dimensional Ising model.

Block-spin coarse-graining (SB​=sgn∑i∈B​si​)

Words: 201
Renormalization group OurBigBook.com
Consider Ising spins si​=±1 on a square lattice of spacing a. Divide it into disjoint 3×3 blocks B and retain the majority sign SB​. Each block contains nine spins, so a tie is impossible. For example, five positive and four negative spins produce SB​=+1. All 29 configurations are assigned a retained sign; the individual pattern within a block is lost. A coarse-grained variable has fewer possible values than the microscopic configuration it summarizes.
The spacing between block centres is 3a. In coordinates x′=x/3 it is again a, so the retained pattern can be compared with the original lattice at the same numerical cutoff. This coordinate change does not physically shrink the sample. A majority picture alone does not specify the new interactions: the blocking kernel and original Boltzmann weights determine their probabilities. The figure is a constructed configuration, not a simulated equilibrium state or a claim that majority blocking closes the nearest-neighbour Ising model.

Use a dimensionless statistical Hamiltonian H=H/(kB​T), so that the partition function is Z=∑s​e−H(s). Choose a normalized blocking kernel B(S∣s) with ∑S​B(S∣s)=1. For the majority example it is one when every block has its prescribed majority, and zero otherwise. Define the coarse statistical Hamiltonian by the displayed sum. Then an elementary interchange of finite sums proves
Z′=∑S​e−H′(S)=∑s​e−H(s)∑S​B(S∣s)=Z.
(48)
The probability of a retained pattern is therefore its original marginal probability. For any observable A(S) of the retained variables,
⟨A⟩′=Z1​∑s​e−H(s)∑S​B(S∣s)A(S).
(49)
This is the sense in which elimination preserves predictions for retained information. It does not reconstruct every microscopic observable from a block sign.
Next express positions in units of the enlarged spacing: x′=x/b, where b>1. In a continuum version, rescale the retained scalar field as well to restore a chosen gradient energy coefficient; any change in the integration measure contributes to the field-independent term. The result is a new set of dimensionless couplings. Repeating the procedure defines a renormalization-group flow. Additional interactions and the additive constant generally appear, even if the starting statistical Hamiltonian was simple. Keeping only a few terms is an approximation; the equality of partition functions above applies to the complete coarse weight. See also the Wilsonian coarse-grained statistical Hamiltonian for integration over fast Fourier modes.

For the chosen ϵ=1/5, take two starting models with g0​=1/20 and g0​=3/5. At b=1024, e−ϵℓ=1/4, so their couplings are respectively 4/35 and 6/25. Both move toward 1/5, from opposite sides. They are still visibly different: slow decay of an irrelevant operator can leave substantial corrections at accessible lengths. The case g0​=0 stays exactly zero and is outside this positive-coupling basin.

Renormalization group OurBigBook.com

A relevant operator direction grows and must be tuned to study the same critical behavior. This is a mechanism for losing microscopic detail, not an assertion that every parameter disappears. Critical temperature, individual amplitudes and regular contributions to free energy can remain material dependent.
For the solvable example, write A=ϵ/g0​−1. Its exact solution gives g−ϵ=−ϵAb−ϵ+O(b−2ϵ). At the thermal stopping scale b∗​=∣t0​∣−1/yt​ this is of order ∣t0​∣ϵ/yt​. If the stopped correlation length is smooth in g, the leading correction to its power law has that order. Thus two microscopic couplings can yield the same limiting critical exponent, yet approach it at different rates.
This mechanism makes universality useful: one tractable representative can predict critical exponents and normalized scaling forms for many systems in its universality class. A liquid-gas critical point and a scalar magnetic transition can share a long-distance description even though their microscopic constituents differ. The scope must be checked: spatial dimension, order parameter symmetry, interaction range, and extra soft variables can change the renormalization-group fixed point.

Renormalization-group relevance

Words: 276 Articles: 6
Renormalization group OurBigBook.com
The relevance of a perturbation is determined by the eigenvalue of its dimensionless coupling under linearized renormalization-group flow. Positive, negative and zero eigenvalues define relevant, irrelevant and marginal perturbations, respectively.

Relevant operator

Words: 197 Articles: 2
Renormalization-group relevance OurBigBook.com
An operator is relevant at a fixed point when its coupling has positive renormalization-group eigenvalue. Its dimensionless coupling grows under coarse-graining and drives the theory away from the fixed point unless tuned.
Relevant direction of a fixed point
Words: 165 Articles: 1
Relevant operator OurBigBook.com
A perturbation of a renormalization-group fixed point is relevant if it grows as the coarse-graining length increases. For a continuous flow dδg/dℓ=Mδg, an eigenvector of the linearized matrix with eigenvalue σ grows as eσℓ; a positive real part is relevant, a negative real part is irrelevant and a zero real part requires nonlinear analysis. For a discrete transformation with length factor b>1, its Jacobian matrix multiplier λ instead gives δgn​=λnδg0​: ∣λ∣>1 is relevant, ∣λ∣<1 is irrelevant and ∣λ∣=1 requires nonlinear analysis. For a positive multiplier the scaling exponent is y=logλ/logb. Thus a positive discrete eigenvalue smaller than one is an irrelevant operator direction, while the sign criterion belongs to the continuous generator.

Words: 54
Relevant direction of a fixed point OurBigBook.com
A discrete renormalization group with length factor b>1 and positive relevant thermal multiplier λt​>1 sends t to λt​t and the correlation length to ξ/b. Combining this with ξ∼∣t∣−ν gives the displayed correlation-length critical exponent. The corresponding scaling dimension is yt​=logλt​/logb=1/ν. Relevance of discrete multipliers is determined by magnitude relative to one, unlike the sign criterion for continuous-flow eigenvalues.

An operator is irrelevant at a fixed point when its coupling has negative renormalization-group eigenvalue. Its dimensionless coupling decreases under coarse-graining.

An operator is marginal at linear order when its coupling has zero renormalization-group eigenvalue. Nonlinear terms in its renormalization-group beta function determine whether it is marginally relevant, marginally irrelevant, or exactly marginal.

Systems belong to one universality class when their long-distance renormalization-group flows approach the same fixed point.

Under the scaling hypothesis for critical phenomena, Fs​=Af​∣at​t∣D/yt​Φ±​(0) at zero field. The common free-energy and thermal metric factors cancel from A+​/A−​, leaving a property of the universality class. Universality class OurBigBook.com
When the singular free-energy density has Fs​=Af​∣at​t∣2−αΦ±​(0), the same thermal and free-energy metric factors multiply the singular heat capacity above and below the critical point. Their ratio cancels these factors and depends only on the normalized scaling functions of the universality class. This statement concerns singular amplitudes, not regular heat-capacity backgrounds, and needs separate treatment at logarithmic resonances or zero amplitudes. Branch matching constants belong to the fixed-point scaling functions and cannot be chosen as independent nonuniversal parameters.

Percolation universality hypothesis

Words: 45
Universality class OurBigBook.com
Ordinary short-range independent bond percolation and site percolation on regular lattices of the same spatial dimension are expected to share their percolation critical exponents and large-scale limiting behavior. Their percolation critical probabilities can differ. Long-range or correlated models can lie in a different universality class. A theorem for one lattice alone does not establish this transfer.

If magnetic data collapse with independently specified critical exponents β,γ, the ordinary scaling identities infer Δ=β+γ, δ=1+γ/β, and the displayed exponents. The Fisher scaling relation then gives η=2−γ/ν. These are conditional inferences, not five additional independent measurements. Hyperscaling is needed for the spatial exponents, and subtraction can make small inferred α or η unusually sensitive to uncertainty. A slope on linear axes is not a fitted logarithmic exponent.

A gapless mode associated with a canonically paired pair of broken symmetry generators. In an isotropic ferromagnet, the nonzero expectation of [Sx,Sy]=iSz makes two transverse coordinates one dynamical pair, giving one quadratic magnon branch. Broken-generator counting without this pairing would incorrectly predict two independent modes. This contrasts with the linear phase mode of a superfluid.

Phase stiffness (ρs​)

Words: 109
Goldstone-mode effective free energy OurBigBook.com
The phase stiffness is the coefficient of 21​∫ddx(∇θ)2 in the long-distance free energy. Its renormalized value determines the thermal phase fluctuations and algebraic correlation function of a two-dimensional O(N) model with N=2.
Operationally impose a small phase difference ϕ between opposite sides of a square sample of side L. The smooth minimum has θ=ϕx/L, so the two-dimensional excess free energy is
F(ϕ)−F(0)=21​ρs​ϕ2+o(ϕ2),ρs​=∂ϕ2∂2F​​ϕ=0​.
(58)
The derivative concerns a prescribed twist at the stated observation scale; in d dimensions its conventional size factor is Ld−2. This response definition includes thermal fluctuations and vortices after equilibration, whereas a microscopic gradient coefficient need not. A finite phase stiffness requires no nonzero spatially uniform order parameter; the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition is the instructive example.

Words: 80
Phase-difference variance OurBigBook.com
Fix the uniform order-parameter phase and retain finite system size L before evaluating a massless Gaussian functional integral. In d≤2, its coincident and separated order-parameter phase covariances each acquire a divergent additive constant as L→∞. Their difference 2[GL​(0)−GL​(r)] instead has a finite fixed-separation limit for d>0. This is why physical XY model correlations are obtained from Gaussian phase averaging of angle differences. An ultraviolet cutoff also remains necessary for coincident-point quantities; infrared cancellation does not remove it. The logarithmic two-dimensional Green function follows from the d→2 power-law expression only after subtracting its constant pole.

For the Gaussian functional integral with dimensionless phase stiffness K and a microscopic cutoff a, the Gaussian phase averaging identity gives the displayed correlation function. In two dimensions the phase-difference variance is (πK)−1log(r/a)+O(1), so the XY model has algebraic spin wave correlations with exponent 1/(2πK). In one dimension the variance is r/K, giving exponential decay. Above two dimensions the variance has a finite large-distance limit within the low-temperature spin wave approximation. The Laplacian Green function solves −K∇2G=δ; integration over a sphere fixes G(r)=r2−d/[(d−2)Sd​K]+C for d=2 and G(r)=−(2πK)−1log(r/a)+C for d=2. A mobile spin-triplet excitation above a singlet background in a quantum magnet. At low density, an appropriate triplet branch can be described as bosonic quasiparticles with an effective mass and repulsive interaction. Applied magnetic field can lower one branch toward condensation. The term does not imply that the total excitation number is conserved on thermodynamic timescales.
Linear spin-wave approximation
Words: 332 Articles: 5
Spin wave OurBigBook.com
The linear spin-wave approximation expands a Holstein–Primakoff transformation about a classical ordered state and retains the quadratic oscillator Hamiltonian. It gives the leading order-S excitation energies above the order-S2 classical energy. In a Heisenberg antiferromagnet, first make a bipartite spin rotation. The approximation also predicts a zero-point reduction of the order parameter; infrared-divergent quantum depletion of Néel order signals that the assumed ordered state is not a valid thermodynamic starting point.
Isotropic spin-wave vacuum energy comparison
Words: 63
Linear spin-wave approximation OurBigBook.com
The polarized ground state of an isotropic Heisenberg model with ferromagnetic exchange is an exact state. Its normal-ordered harmonic Hamiltonian has no pair-creation terms, no vacuum magnon occupation and no additional zero-point shift. An antiferromagnetic Néel state instead generates anomalous terms, a squeezed Bogoliubov transformation vacuum, a negative energy correction and reduced staggered magnetization. Neither statement licenses omitting normal-ordering constants from an arbitrary spin-wave model with anisotropy or a different reference state.

In one dimension its logarithmic infrared divergence invalidates finite ordered magnetization and prevents the linear approximation from deciding the exact gap.

Folding the magnetic zone separates the gapless in-plane mode from the gapped out-of-plane polarization. An easy-axis reference in this regime is unstable and does not supply this physical expansion.
